Galleria dell’Accademia

The must-sees

11 places Wizzy will tap you for first, each with a story and something to look for.

  1. 01
    Church

    Baptistery of St. John

    Generations of Florentines, Dante among them, were baptised here. Lorenzo Ghiberti spent decades on its bronze doors; the east pair became known as the Gates of Paradise, and copies now hang in place of the originals.

    Look for

    On the frame of the Gates of Paradise, find Ghiberti’s own small bald head peering out among the prophets.

  2. 02
    Church

    Basilica of Santa Croce

    Its chapels are painted by Giotto and his followers, and Dante has a monument here though he is buried in Ravenna. The flood of 1966 badly damaged Cimabue’s great Crucifix in the church museum.

    Look for

    High on the 19th-century façade is a Star of David, placed there by its Jewish architect, Niccolò Matas.

  3. 03
    Church

    Basilica of Santa Maria Novella

    Leon Battista Alberti completed the facade in the 15th century for the Rucellai family. Inside is Masaccio’s Trinity, one of the first paintings to use true linear perspective.

    Look for

    On the façade, find an armillary sphere and a sundial, put up in the 1570s to track the equinox for the calendar.

  4. 04
    Church · 1436

    Florence Cathedral

    Filippo Brunelleschi built the dome without the usual wooden scaffolding from the ground, using a double shell of brick. The cathedral was consecrated in 1436, and the facade was only finished in the 19th century.

    Look for

    Inside, above the main door, Paolo Uccello’s clock shows 24 hours and its hand runs anticlockwise.

  5. 05
    Museum

    Galleria dell’Accademia

    Michelangelo finished the David in 1504 and it stood outside the Palazzo Vecchio for more than three centuries. It was moved indoors here in 1873 to protect it; his unfinished Prisoners line the hall leading up to it.

    Look for

    The head and hands are oversized: the statue was first meant to stand high on the cathedral, seen from far below.

  6. 06
    Palace

    Palazzo Pitti

    Begun for the banker Luca Pitti, it was bought in 1550 by Eleonora di Toledo, wife of Cosimo I, and became the main Medici residence. Later the Lorraine grand dukes and, briefly, the kings of Italy lived here.

    Look for

    At the edge of the Boboli Gardens, near the palace, Morgante, a dwarf of Cosimo I’s court, sits naked astride a turtle in a fountain.

  7. 07
    Civic building

    Palazzo Vecchio

    Built from 1299 for the city’s government, it later became the Medici residence before they moved across the river. It is still Florence’s town hall, and its vast Hall of the Five Hundred was decorated by Vasari.

    Look for

    On the façade’s right-hand corner, near the door, a man’s profile is scratched into the stone. Legend says Michelangelo carved it.

  8. 08
    Square

    Piazza della Signoria

    A round plaque in the paving marks where the preacher Girolamo Savonarola was burned in 1498. Ammannati’s Neptune Fountain stands at the corner, nicknamed il Biancone, the big white one.

    Look for

    In the open loggia at the corner, Cellini’s bronze Perseus holds up the severed head of Medusa.

  9. 09
    Viewpoint

    Piazzale Michelangelo

    Giuseppe Poggi designed it in the 1860s, when Florence was briefly capital of Italy. A bronze copy of David stands in the middle, surrounded by copies of Michelangelo’s Medici Chapel figures.

    Look for

    Turn uphill to find San Miniato al Monte, the green and white marble church above the terrace.

  10. 10
    Bridge · 1345

    Ponte Vecchio

    Butchers and tanners once worked on the bridge until Ferdinando I de’ Medici replaced them with goldsmiths in 1593. In 1944 the retreating German army blew up every other bridge in the city but spared this one.

    Look for

    In the open middle of the bridge, a bust of the goldsmith Benvenuto Cellini looks out from his pedestal.

  11. 11
    Museum

    Uffizi Gallery

    Giorgio Vasari designed the building in the 1560s as offices, uffizi, for Cosimo I de’ Medici’s government. The last Medici, Anna Maria Luisa, left the family’s art to the city on condition it never leave Florence.

    Look for

    In the niches of the courtyard stand statues of great Tuscans, among them Dante, Leonardo, Michelangelo and Galileo.
